summary: These four test methods check the RobotPet.charge method from every angle: adding charge, adding so much that it hits the 100 maximum, passing a negative amount to drain the battery, and draining past the 0 minimum. Each one sets the battery to a known starting value, calls charge, and asserts the resulting battery level.

lines.text: Each test method's name states the behaviour being checked, so a failure report tells you what broke without you having to read the code. The name must start with test_ for unittest to find and run it.
This is the arrange step: the shared pet created in setUp is put into a known starting state so the expected result is predictable. Never rely on whatever battery level a previous test left behind.
The act step calls the one method under test. Notice that charge changes the object rather than returning a value, so the assertion has to inspect the object afterwards.
The assert step compares the battery attribute against the value you worked out by hand, 50 + 20. If charge did anything else, the test fails and prints both numbers.
Testing the boundary is as important as testing the normal case, because capping logic is exactly where off-by-one mistakes hide.
Charging 90 by 50 would give 140, which is impossible for a percentage, so this call forces the upper limit to do its job.
The expected value is the cap rather than the arithmetic total, which is what makes this a test of the limit.
A negative argument is a legitimate use of charge in this design, so it deserves its own test rather than being left as an accident that happens to work.
Passing a negative amount drains the battery, reusing the same method instead of needing a separate discharge method.
This is the mirror image of the cap test: draining 10 by 50 must stop at 0 instead of going negative.
Zero, not -40, is the correct answer, and asserting it locks the lower bound into place so a future edit cannot quietly remove it.
